finalText:
An `async` or `defer` attribute on a classic external script means the browser fetches it in parallel with HTML parsing. The two differ in when the script runs. `defer` runs it after parsing finishes and before `DOMContentLoaded`, in document order. `async` runs it as soon as it has downloaded, in no guaranteed order.

**Parsing and execution timing**
- `async`: The HTML Standard says "if the async attribute is present, then the classic script will be fetched in parallel to parsing and evaluated as soon as it is available (potentially before parsing completes)." (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html) So it can interrupt the parser while it executes, but it never waits for parsing to finish.
- `defer`: The same page says the script "will be fetched in parallel and evaluated when the page has finished parsing." MDN adds that a deferred script is "meant to be executed after the document has been parsed, but before firing DOMContentLoaded event." (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script)
- With neither attribute, the script "is fetched and evaluated immediately, blocking parsing until these are both complete." (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html)

**Relation to `DOMContentLoaded`**
- Deferred scripts hold the event back. MDN says they "will prevent the DOMContentLoaded event from firing until the script has loaded and finished evaluating." (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script)
- The `DOMContentLoaded` page confirms that the event "doesn't wait for other things like images, subframes, and async scripts to finish loading." (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/DOMContentLoaded_event)
- An `async` script can therefore run before or after the event. It runs before if it arrives while parsing is still going. It runs after if it arrives later. Code in an async script should check `document.readyState` before waiting for `DOMContentLoaded`.
- The sources differ slightly here. A note on the MDN event page says `DOMContentLoaded` "is fired after the execution of these scripts, but before the execution of scripts with async". That reads as if async scripts always come after. The spec text (`async` may run "potentially before parsing completes") and the same page's remark that an async script may run before or after the event show that the order is not fixed. I treat the order as a race that depends on network timing.

**Order with several scripts**
- `defer`: MDN says "Scripts with the defer attribute will execute in the order in which they appear in the document." (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script) In the spec's processing model, parser-inserted deferred scripts, and module scripts without `async`, are appended to a "list of scripts that will execute when the document has finished parsing". That is an ordered list.
- `async`: The processing model puts these scripts in a "set of scripts that will execute as soon as possible". Each one executes when its own result is ready. The spec states no ordering for that set, so whichever script finishes downloading first runs first. This is my reading of the data structure. I did not find an explicit "async is unordered" sentence in the pages I opened.
- If both attributes are present, `async` wins. MDN says "the element will act as if only the async attribute is specified." The spec says `defer` may be added alongside `async` so that legacy browsers without `async` support fall back to deferred behavior rather than blocking.
- Scripts added dynamically (not parser-inserted) go into a separate "list of scripts that will execute in order as soon as possible" unless they have `async`. The spec's "force async" flag makes parser-inserted scripts that failed to run behave as async if they are later executed.

**Inline classic scripts**
- Both attributes do nothing here. MDN warns that each "must not be used if the src attribute is absent (i.e., for inline scripts), in this case it would have no effect." (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script)
- The spec only runs the async/defer branches for a classic script with `src`, or for a module. Otherwise it will "immediately execute the script element el, even if other scripts are already executing." (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html)

**`type="module"` scripts**
- Modules are deferred by default. The spec says that, without `async`, "the module script and its dependencies will be fetched in parallel to parsing and evaluated when the page has finished parsing. (The defer attribute has no effect on module scripts.)" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/scripting.html) MDN agrees: "The defer attribute has no effect on module scripts — they defer by default."
- With `async`, the module and all its dependencies are fetched in parallel, and it is "evaluated as soon as it is available (potentially before parsing completes)". It then has the same unordered, race-with-`DOMContentLoaded` behavior as an async classic script.
- Inline modules differ from inline classic scripts. The spec's processing model sends every module through the async/defer branches, including inline ones. The spec's inline module example says such a script "will not be evaluated until both document parsing has complete and its dependency (dom-utils.mjs) has been fetched and evaluated." So an inline module is deferred. With `async` it runs once its imports are ready.
- Deferred and module scripts both count toward `DOMContentLoaded`. MDN says the event waits for "all deferred scripts (<script defer src="…"> and <script type="module">)".

**Sources**
- The cited MDN script page, MDN `DOMContentLoaded` page and spec section were all opened and read.
- I could not open the javascript.info page (404). I did not use the web.dev search results, since I never opened them.
